paras: The beating of Daniel Mack was the removal of a recently discharged Black soldier from the town lockup at Sylvester, Worth County, Georgia, by armed white men, who beat him severely, on a Monday night in spring 1919 shortly before May 3. The fullest report said Mack survived with a fractured skull and was hidden by his relatives, while other Black papers reported him beaten to death or 'believed lynched.' Black weeklies treated the attack as a case of a returned soldier abused in the South.

Mack, whom the Chicago Defender called 'Daniel Muck' and a veteran of the 365th Infantry who had served overseas, was in a confrontation with a white man on a crowded street in Sylvester. According to the New York Age, he knocked down a white man who had bumped into him; the Defender said he remarked that he had fought for the white man in France and would stand for no mistreatment. Tried in the mayor's court, he was sentenced to thirty days on the streets, and the Defender added that he was jailed in his army uniform with shackles on his legs.

After Mack had served part of the sentence, four armed men overpowered the acting night marshal, took his keys and removed Mack from the lockup on a Monday night. The Defender described the men as friends of the white man and said they beat Mack over the head with oak sticks, carried him near a small town a few miles away and beat him again. The New York Age reported that he was badly mutilated and his skull fractured.

Mack could not be found afterward; the New York Age explained that his relatives, fearing further trouble, had spirited him away. The same report said feeling in Sylvester was strong against the attackers and that prominent men of the town promised vigorous prosecution if they could be located. No report of arrests, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

Only Black papers carried the story in the coverage examined, beginning with a special to the New York Age from Albany, Georgia, on May 3 headed 'Want assailants of soldier punished.' The Chicago Defender followed on May 10 with a Sylvester dispatch whose lead said Mack had been beaten to death, though its text said only that no trace of him had been found. On May 17 the Cleveland Gazette rewrote the Age story under the head 'Mutilate Soldier!' beneath a banner reading 'Our overseas soldiers beaten and mutilated in the Southland!' The Gazette called the attackers 'white brutes' and closed by calling the beating Georgia's 'recompensation' to soldiers who went overseas to fight for 'democracy.'

A shorter Associated Negro Press brief, datelined Moultrie, May 14, gave a different picture: a mob of about thirty men in automobiles, and a fate left open between a thrashing with orders to leave the county and lynching. The Baltimore Afro-American ran it on May 16 as 'Another Georgian believed lynched,' the Omaha Monitor on May 17 as 'Former soldier probably lynched,' and the Kansas City Sun on May 24 as 'Negro Soldier "Lost."'

The accounts differ on the size of the attacking party, four armed men in the New York Age and Defender against about thirty in the ANP brief. They differ also on Mack's fate: the Age said he survived and was hidden by relatives, the Defender's lead said he was beaten to death, and the ANP brief said no one knew. The Age report is the earliest and most detailed and accounts for his disappearance, while the later ANP brief was filed from Moultrie and reported rumor on both sides.

reader.title: Beating of Daniel Mack
bases: Armed white men took Mack from the town lockup and beat him severely; the fullest report says he survived and was taken away by relatives (A1), while the Defender said he was beaten to death (A2) and the ANP brief that his fate was unknown (A3).

Three independent Black-press reports, the New York Age special (A1), the Defender's Sylvester dispatch (A2) and the Associated Negro Press brief (A3), agree that a discharged soldier named Mack was taken from the Sylvester jail by white men, though they differ on numbers and outcome.

accounts.label: New York Age correspondent (Albany, Ga.)
accounts.gist: Four armed men overpowered the acting night marshal and took Mack from the lockup; he was badly mutilated with a fractured skull, and his relatives spirited him away. Local feeling ran against the attackers and prosecution was promised.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender (Sylvester dispatch)
accounts.gist: Four armed friends of the white man stormed the jail, beat Mack with oak sticks, carried him near a nearby town and beat him again; the lead says he was beaten to death, and no trace of him had been found.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press (Moultrie)
accounts.gist: A mob of about thirty men in automobiles removed Mack from the Sylvester jail; some thought he was thrashed and told to leave the county, others that he was lynched.

framing.detail: The New York Age headlined 'Want assailants of soldier punished' and stressed local feeling against the attackers.
The Defender stressed his overseas service, his uniform and shackles, and the oak sticks 'as large as a man's wrist.'
The ANP brief ran as 'Another Georgian believed lynched,' 'Former soldier probably lynched' and 'Negro Soldier "Lost"'.
The Cleveland Gazette ran 'Mutilate Soldier!' under a banner on overseas soldiers 'beaten and mutilated in the Southland,' calling the attackers 'white brutes.'
